title.en: Forty days of fasting for shaming a friend

summary.en: The Mashgiach cites an old mussar sefer that one who shamed his friend in public must appease him and also fast forty days. Since nobody can fast today, he explains, Hashem sends a sincere penitent great mitzvos to repair the blemish, just as He finds ways for a thief who cannot find his victims.

title.en: Worse than murder; Boaz and Manoach

summary.en: The Mashgiach brings the Gemara that one who shames his friend in public has no share in the World to Come, and asks why this is harsher than murder. He then tells the Gemara's account that Boaz lost his sixty children because he never invited Manoach to their weddings, and stresses that a good intention is no excuse for shaming a Jew.

title.en: Kavod habriyos: the met mitzvah and the mizbeach

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains the mitzvah of kavod habriyos, greater still for the dead: a Kohen Gadol on the eve of Yom Kippur who finds a met mitzvah must bury it and lose the Yom Kippur service. He then brings the prohibition of steps to the mizbeach and Rashi's kal vachomer: if the Torah protects the honor of unfeeling stones, how much more a person, so one may not embarrass any Jew, even to teach him a lesson.

title.en: The fearful soldier and Bilam's donkey

summary.en: The Mashgiach brings Rashi that the newly married man and the one who planted a vineyard are sent home from war so that the one who fears his sins is not shamed when he returns. He then brings Rashi that the angel killed Bilam's donkey so it would not be a disgrace to Bilam, and asks how much more one must honor a Jew.

title.en: The chol bird in Noach's teivah

summary.en: The Mashgiach tells the Midrash of the chol bird that hid in a corner of the teivah rather than trouble the busy Noach for food, and was blessed by Noach to live forever. He connects this to the words 'like the chol' and concludes that one never loses through good middos.

title.en: The Ba'al Shem Tov's path and the Chofetz Chaim

summary.en: The Mashgiach describes the new path of the Ba'al Shem Tov, serving Hashem with love and joy, and the opposition of the great misnagdim led by the Vilna Gaon, while later honest Litvaks came to respect the chassidim. He tells, as he heard from talmidim, how the Chofetz Chaim had two grandsons of the Berditchever Rav admitted to his full yeshivah so they would be in his shul on Rosh Hashanah.

title.en: Rabbi Chaim of Volozhin and the cherem

summary.en: The Mashgiach tells how Rabbi Chaim of Volozhin refused to sign the Vilna Gaon's cherem against the chassidim, answering from the akeidah that to harm a Jew an angel is not enough, though to save one even an angel is obeyed. He brings Rabbi Avraham of Slonim's observation that the greatest leaders left a chain of great descendants, and that among the Litvaks only Rabbi Chaim of Volozhin did, because he would not harm a Jew.

oneLiner.en: The Mashgiach explains that Pinchas acted as a simple member of Klal Yisrael, not above it, and sees the same holiness of the Jewish people in the thousands who searched for a lost child this week, closing with emunah in Hashem's hidden reckoning and the comfort of Parshas Pinchas.

abstract.en: The Mashgiach opens with Pinchas, who as a killer should have lost the kehunah yet became a new kohen through his deed. Aharon received kehunah as a gift; Pinchas earned it by atoning for Klal Yisrael. The word 'besocham' shows he did not raise himself above the people: knowing he risked the kehunah, he acted only to sanctify Hashem's name as a simple member of Klal Yisrael, which is why Moshe Rabbeinu, the leader, could not be the one. Zimri was a Jew with a foreign growth attached to him. This week too a Jew fell, while thousands of plain Jews from Boro Park and elsewhere searched all night for a lost child, showing that Jews are merciful, modest and kind. Parshas Pinchas brings comfort before the three weeks, which this rare year it precedes, with the haftorah of Eliyahu. The Mashgiach closes that the reckoning of souls is hidden until Moshiach comes, reads the long Ani Maamin on hashgachah, and calls to be comforted with Shabbos.

en: Aharon received the kehunah as a gift, while Pinchas earned it by atoning for Klal Yisrael, so it passed to his descendants.
'Besocham' teaches that Pinchas did not raise himself above Klal Yisrael; he acted as a simple Jew, a member of the people.
Pinchas knew he risked the kehunah and acted only to sanctify Hashem's name and show that Klal Yisrael has no connection to Zimri.
The thousands of plain Jews who searched all night for a lost child showed what a Jew is: merciful, modest and doing kindness.
Parshas Pinchas, with its moadim and the haftorah of Eliyahu, is a comfort for the Jewish people in the time of the three weeks.
How each soul reaches its tikkun is hidden from us until Moshiach comes; now one must believe that everything was for the good.

title.en: Pinchas earns the kehunah from within Klal Yisrael

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that Pinchas, though a killer is unfit for kehunah, became a new kohen, earning what Aharon got as a gift. From 'besocham' he shows that Pinchas did not set himself above the people but acted as a simple Jew for the sake of kiddush Hashem, which is why Moshe Rabbeinu could not be the one to act.

title.en: Zimri's foreign growth and this week's search

summary.en: The Mashgiach describes Zimri as a Jew to whom something foreign attached itself, and compares a Jew who fell this week. Against that, he describes the thousands of plain Jews who searched all night for a lost child and the kiddush Hashem at the levayah, showing that Jews are merciful, modest and kind.

title.en: Parshas Pinchas as comfort before the three weeks

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that Parshas Pinchas, with its moadim and Eliyahu, comforts the Jewish people in the three weeks, and notes that this rare year it falls before them. He adds that the moadim correspond to the Avos, and that Eliyahu, whose name equals 'ben', will reveal that Jews are Hashem's children.

title.en: Emunah in Hashem's hidden reckoning; comfort of Shabbos

summary.en: The Mashgiach says the tikkun of each soul is a reckoning we cannot grasp until Moshiach comes, and that the child came into the world for his own tikkun. He reads the long version of Ani Maamin on the sufferings of tzaddikim and hashgachah pratis, then closes that this week Klal Yisrael appeared in its glory and one must be comforted with Shabbos.

catalogTitle: עבודה תמה זהו שבירת היצר. שלא לחפוש מנוחה - זהו עבודת אברהם אוהבי. שייכות ענין זה למילה.

oneLiner.en: The Mashgiach explains the Tanya's distinction between the 'oved Elokim', the beinoni who keeps fighting his yetzer hara, and the one who 'has not served Him' because his good conduct costs him no struggle, and stresses that for the beinoni this lifelong struggle is a complete avodah.

abstract.en: The Mashgiach opens Tanya chapter 15 with the verse in Malachi that contrasts tzaddik with rasha and 'oved Elokim' with 'one who has not served Him'. 'Oved' is present tense: the beinoni who is still at war with the yetzer hara over the 'small city' of the body, while 'eved', a noun, is the tzaddik who has already won. He digresses on how much weaker today's generation is, comparing it to a small child whose slips are forgiven, and supports this with the yetzer hara cited before and after the Flood and with Bilaam's blessing that Hashem does not look at wrongdoing in Yaakov. He then defines the beinoni 'who has not served Him': a natural or habituated masmid who does no aveiros but makes no effort beyond his routine, explained through the Gemara of learning a hundred versus a hundred and one times. The beinoni's lifelong struggle is a complete avodah, illustrated by two stories.

en: Tzaddik and rasha form one pair and 'oved Elokim' and 'one who has not served Him' a second pair, both within the level of the beinoni and the tzaddik who is not a rasha.

'Oved' in the present tense describes the beinoni who is in the middle of the war with the yetzer hara, while 'eved', a noun like 'chacham' or 'melech', describes the tzaddik who has already driven it out.
The beinoni 'who has not served Him' does no aveiros and learns constantly, but does it by routine, without fighting his yetzer hara or striving to grow.
Such a person may be a natural masmid, cooled by the black gall, or one who trained himself until learning became second nature; either way he needs only the hidden love of Hashem every Jew has.
Learning a hundred and one times, one more than the accustomed hundred, is what makes one an 'oved Elokim', because it breaks a routine.
For the beinoni, the constant struggle against the yetzer hara until his last breath is a complete avodah; Hashem does not demand that he become a tzaddik.

title.en: Oved Elokim versus eved

summary.en: The Mashgiach opens the chapter with the verse contrasting tzaddik and rasha, oved Elokim and one who has not served Him, and explains that 'oved' is the beinoni still at war with the yetzer hara while 'eved' is the tzaddik who has already won. He then notes that the beinoni himself has two levels.

title.en: A weaker generation, treated gently

summary.en: The Mashgiach digresses on how far the world has fallen since earlier generations, recalling the decent world of his youth, and says that today one must be gentler with talmidim and friends. Like a two-year-old who slips, today's Jews are not held to the old standard; what matters is that they want to do Hashem's will.

title.en: The yetzer hara before and after the Flood

summary.en: The Mashgiach asks how the yetzer hara could be the reason both for bringing the Flood and for never bringing another, and answers that the mighty generations before it were held responsible while the weakened world after it is treated like a sick child. He adds Bilaam's blessing that Hashem does not look at wrongdoing in Yaakov, with Rashi, and distinguishes one who slips while wanting to be good from one who sins in rebellion.

title.en: The beinoni who has not served Him

summary.en: The Mashgiach defines the beinoni 'who has not served Him': he keeps all the mitzvos and learns constantly but by routine, without using Hashem's help to grow. He explains why such a person needs no struggle: he is a natural masmid of cold temperament, or he trained himself until it became second nature, so the hidden love of Hashem suffices.

title.en: A hundred and one times

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains the Gemara that one who reviews a hundred times has not served Him, while one who reviews a hundred and one times has: like the donkey drivers who charge double past the usual distance, the extra time goes beyond the routine. He links a hundred to the gematria of the yetzer hara's name and a hundred and one to the angel Michael, and concludes that the beinoni must always seek to grow, which is his complete avodah.

title.en: The struggle until the last breath

summary.en: Few people kill the yetzer hara; most struggle until their last moment. The Mashgiach tells of a chassid who on his deathbed made a gesture of victory over the yetzer hara, and the Chiddushei HaRim's comment that at that moment he lost the battle. This lifelong struggle is the beinoni's complete avodah.

title.en: The masmid of Koretz and his judgment

summary.en: The Mashgiach tells of a young masmid in Koretz who agreed to divorce rather than stop learning, was brought back by his father-in-law, and after his death reported that he was sentenced to Gehinnom for one fleeting proud thought, a sentence reduced because he accepted it without question. He concludes that if people today were judged this way it would be grim, but the main thing is to truly want to be an oved, and Hashem does not scrutinize those who slip.

oneLiner.en: The Mashgiach explains that Avraham Avinu, the 'third challah' of the world, left his children the inheritance of emunah, and teaches how to make that emunah clear and how to guard it from the thieves who want to steal it.

abstract.en: The Mashgiach opens Parshas Lech Lecha with a mashal of a woman whose Shabbos challos fail to rise twice and succeed the third time. Adam HaRishon was the 'challah of the world' and did not succeed; neither did the world after Noach; the third challah, Avraham Avinu, succeeded, and from him came the Jewish people. His legacy to his children is emunah, first mentioned in the Torah by him. Every Jew believes, but most have a dim emunah rather than a clear one; clear emunah means knowing that Hashem is here and sees everything, and it grows through Torah, mitzvos and tefillah. Emunah, heard at Sinai from Hashem Himself, is a precious diamond that the yetzer hara wants to steal. The Mashgiach gives three ways to guard it: keep away from apikorsus, do not get caught up in politics as if people run the world, and believe that all Hashem does is good even when one cannot understand, like Avraham at the Akeidah.

en: Adam HaRishon, and then the world of Noach, were 'challos' that did not succeed; Avraham Avinu was the third challah that did, and from him came the Jewish people who will enter the day that is entirely Shabbos.
The inheritance Avraham Avinu gave his children is emunah, and every Jew, even one who claims he does not believe, truly believes.
Most people have emunah that is dim rather than clear; clear emunah means knowing that Hashem is here and sees and knows everything, and it grows with more Torah, mitzvos and tefillah.
Emunah is a precious diamond, heard directly from Hashem at Sinai, and the yetzer hara and his forces try to steal it, or at least a piece of it, so it must be guarded.

The Mashgiach gives three ways of guarding emunah: keeping away from apikorsim, not being drawn into political talk that forgets that Hashem runs the world, and believing that everything Hashem does is for the good.
Avraham's test at the Akeidah was not the sacrifice itself but that he could have had a kushya, and he went with joy to do Hashem's will without looking at it.

title.en: Avraham Avinu, the third challah of the world

summary.en: The Mashgiach tells a mashal of a woman whose Shabbos challos fail twice and rise the third time, and applies it: Adam HaRishon, the 'challah of the world', and the world after Noach did not succeed, while Avraham Avinu, the third challah, did. Avraham's inheritance to his children is emunah.

title.en: Every Jew believes: dim emunah and clear emunah

summary.en: The Mashgiach says every Jew believes, even one who says he does not, and that the first mention of emunah is by Avraham. He distinguishes dim from clear emunah, which means knowing Hashem is present and watching, and says that clear emunah would keep a person from sinning, so one must work on it.

title.en: Emunah, a diamond that thieves want to steal

summary.en: The Mashgiach calls emunah the most precious diamond, the foundation of all mitzvos, since the first two of the Ten Commandments were heard from Hashem Himself. The yetzer hara and his forces want to steal it, as the Satan took it from Adam and Chava, so emunah must be guarded.

title.en: Guarding emunah: apikorsim and politics

summary.en: The first safeguard is to keep away from even a 'small apikores' and not to argue with him, since such words are poison. The second is not to get caught up in political talk, like the talk about the presidential election, as if the president runs the world; one may daven and make hishtadlus, as for parnassah, but must know that Hashem alone leads the world.

title.en: Believing that all Hashem does is good

summary.en: The third safeguard is to believe that everything Hashem does is for the good. The Mashgiach raises the question of the suffering righteous and the prospering wicked, which Moshe Rabbeinu wanted to understand and which Yirmiyahu asked while declaring Hashem righteous, and explains that a tzaddik may suffer to repair what he damaged in an earlier gilgul. He opens the example of the bondage in Egypt.

title.en: Gilgulim in Egypt and in later decrees

summary.en: The Mashgiach brings the Arizal that the Jews in Egypt were souls of the generation of the flood and of the dispersion, punished measure for measure: bricks and mortar for those who built the tower, the river for those of the flood. He adds that tzaddikim revealed that the victims of the decrees of Tach v'Tat were the biryonim of the Churban, and that today, without ruach hakodesh, one must still know that all is by Hashem's just reckoning.

title.en: The test of the Akeidah: serving despite a kushya

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that Avraham's test at the Akeidah was not giving up his son, which idol worshippers also did, but serving Hashem with joy despite the kushya that Yitzchak was promised as his heir. A non-Jew can sacrifice but cannot bear a kushya; a Jew knows Hashem is righteous whether or not he understands, and that in the end all will be seen as good.

oneLiner.en: Starting from the Ba'al Shem Tov's reading of 'make a light for the teivah' as making the word of prayer shine, the Mashgiach teaches the bachurim that tefillah, said slowly, aloud and with the whole heart, is the ark that saves a Jew from the flood of this world.

abstract.en: The Mashgiach opens with the Ba'al Shem Tov on Parshas Noach: the teivah is the word of prayer, which one must fill with light and enter with one's whole being. Through his rebbe he ties this to the plain meaning: the world is a flood of desires, and as Noach was saved by the ark, a Jew is saved by davening, above all a long morning davening. He tells how a camp minyan of bachurim who davened slowly grew into the shul's minyan, and explains with the Gemara why tefillah, though it stands at the height of the world, is mocked. He then reads the Ramban at the end of Parshas Bo: the world was created so that people gather in shuls and proclaim aloud that they are His creations, and loud davening overpowers the yetzer hara. From the Ba'al HaTanya's letters he shows the call for slow chazzanim and long davening, and closes that in the time before Moshiach the main avodah is tefillah with the whole heart, alongside learning.

en: The Ba'al Shem Tov reads 'make a light for the teivah' as making each word of prayer shine, and 'come into the teivah with all your household' as putting one's whole self into the words.
The world is a flood of desires and pursuit of honor in which most people drown, and as Noach was saved by the ark, a Jew is saved by davening, especially a long morning davening.
According to the Ramban, Hashem created the world so that people gather in shuls and proclaim aloud that they are His creations, which is the purpose of raising the voice in prayer.

The Ba'al HaTanya asks that the weekday chazzan be someone with time, who can daven shacharis for at least an hour and a half, and he is pained by those who push a long-davening chazzan away from the amud.
Davening fast without kavanah fulfills only the rabbinic mitzvah of tefillah, not the Torah mitzvah of serving Hashem with all one's heart.
In the generations before Moshiach the main avodah is tefillah, though bachurim must still learn all day, since the start of a person's life, like the start of the world, belongs to Torah.

title.en: The teivah is the word of prayer

summary.en: The Mashgiach brings the Ba'al Shem Tov's reading of 'make a light for the teivah' as filling the word of prayer with light and entering it with everything one has. He asks how this drush fits the plain meaning and answers with his rebbe's teaching that the world is a flood, and as Noach was saved by the ark a Jew is saved by davening, above all in the morning.

title.en: A bachurim minyan, and why prayer is mocked

summary.en: The Mashgiach tells how, as rosh hamasmidim in camp, he organized young bachurim to daven slowly in the morning, and how their request to continue in the city became the minyan of the shul. He then asks why someone who learns well is honored while someone who davens well is mocked, and answers with the Gemara that tefillah is among the things that stand at the height of the world yet people treat lightly.

title.en: The Ramban: prayer is the purpose of creation

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that reading a holy sefer in the author's own words is as if the author stands before the reader, and then reads the Ramban at the end of Parshas Bo. The Ramban writes that the purpose of the mitzvos and of creation is that people recognize Hashem as their Creator, thank Him and turn to Him in prayer.

title.en: Davening aloud, in shul, against the yetzer hara

summary.en: Continuing the Ramban, the Mashgiach explains that shuls and loud prayer exist so that people gather and proclaim before Hashem that they are His creations, and brings the Yerushalmi on the people of Nineveh that prayer needs a voice. He adds that loud davening overpowers the yetzer hara, who urges a quick davening, and brings Reb Aharon of Karlin that simple people must daven aloud, as is the custom in Stolin.

title.en: The Ba'al HaTanya's letter on the chazzan

summary.en: The Mashgiach reads a letter of the Ba'al HaTanya asking that working men not lead the weekday davening, but melamdim and kollel yungeleit who can daven shacharis for at least an hour and a half, chosen by lot or by the majority, with the others surrounding the chazzan. He adds that in his shul the best places around the amud are given to the bachurim, who still have freshness in davening.

title.en: Don't drive away the long-davening chazzan

summary.en: From a second letter, the Mashgiach explains why the Ba'al HaTanya was pained by people who push a slow chazzan from the amud: one who lengthens his prayer lengthens his days, and they drive away that life. He tells of the Chasam Sofer's answer to a friend about long davening, and concludes that a person who must hurry to work should rather leave, even without hearing kedushah, than rush the chazzan, applying this to his own yungeleit.

title.en: Prayer with the whole heart before Moshiach

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that fast davening without kavanah fulfills only the rabbinic mitzvah, not the Torah mitzvah of serving Hashem with all one's heart, and brings the Shulchan Aruch on kavanah in the first berachah. He returns to the Ba'al HaTanya: in the time before Moshiach the main avodah is tefillah, while bachurim must still learn, and in davening the hidden love of Hashem in every Jew comes out.

oneLiner.en: Through Yosef and his brothers, Tamar and Potifar's wife, a story of the Sanzer Rav and the Midrash on Amalek, the Mashgiach teaches that one must never shame or ruin another Jew, since even a deed meant for the sake of Heaven is wicked without good middos.

abstract.en: The Mashgiach opens with Yosef sending everyone out before revealing himself, so as not to shame his brothers. He explains that the shevatim, each bound to a combination of Hashem's Name, judged Yosef in beis din as a rodef, and brings the Midrash Tanchuma that some events, like Adam's sin, Moshe's failure at Mei Merivah and the sale of Yosef, had to happen. Yosef therefore risked his life to spare his brothers shame. Rashi says Tamar and Potifar's wife both meant it for the sake of Heaven, yet Potifar's wife is called wicked: Tamar risked her life not to shame Yehuda, while the other had bad middos and libeled Yosef. The Mashgiach applies this to shaming someone who talks during davening, tells of the Sanzer Rav and a business competitor, and explains through a Midrash mashal why Hashem blames Amalek rather than Israel's doubt. He closes with kavod habriyos, love of a Jew as love of Hashem, and a story of the Belzer Rav.

en: Yosef sent everyone out before revealing himself so as not to shame his brothers, even though he thereby put his own life in danger.
The brothers did not act wantonly: they held a beis din and ruled that Yosef had the status of a rodef.
According to the Midrash, certain events were decreed by Hashem and those involved had no real choice, among them the sale of Yosef.
One can act for the sake of Heaven and still be a great rasha if one lacks good middos; the difference between Tamar and Potifar's wife was that Tamar refused to shame Yehuda.
It is no mitzvah to ruin a Jew who is not a tzaddik; rebuke must be given pleasantly and in a friendly way.
Love of a fellow Jew is bound up with love of Hashem, as hinted by the equal gematria of the two verses of 've'ahavta'.

title.en: Yosef spares his brothers shame

summary.en: The Mashgiach brings Rashi that Yosef sent everyone out so his brothers would not be shamed, and explains that the shevatim, each bound to a combination of Hashem's Name, judged Yosef in beis din as a rodef.

title.en: Events Hashem decrees, and Yosef's risk

summary.en: From the Midrash Tanchuma the Mashgiach explains that Adam's sin, Moshe's failure at Mei Merivah and the sale of Yosef had to happen. He then brings the Midrash that Yosef risked being killed by sending everyone out, rather than shame his brothers.

title.en: Tamar and Potifar's wife: middos decide

summary.en: The Mashgiach brings Rashi that Tamar and Potifar's wife both acted for the sake of Heaven, and asks why the latter is called a rasha. He answers that Tamar had good middos and would not shame Yehuda, while Potifar's wife libeled Yosef, and applies this to shaming someone who talks during davening.

title.en: The Sanzer Rav and the competitor

summary.en: The Mashgiach tells of a man in Sanz who claimed it was a mitzvah to ruin a competitor who was not a proper Jew, and of the Sanzer Rav's proof from the darkness in Egypt that it is no mitzvah. He concludes that rebuke must be given pleasantly.

title.en: Amalek and the king's dog

summary.en: The Mashgiach asks why Hashem says 'remember what Amalek did' rather than reminding Israel of their doubt 'is Hashem among us'. He brings the Midrash's mashal of a king whose thieving friend was bitten by the guard dogs, and who blamed the dog so as not to shame his friend.

title.en: Kavod habriyos and love of a Jew

summary.en: The Mashgiach shows the weight of kavod habriyos from the laws of interrupting kerias shema, and brings the remez that the verses of love of Hashem and love of one's fellow are equal in gematria. He mentions the yahrzeit of Rabbi Yissachar Dov of Belz.

title.en: The Belzer Rav's cry on Rosh Hashana

summary.en: The Mashgiach tells of a boy who had strayed and stood outside chatting on Rosh Hashana in Belz, and became a baal teshuvah when he heard the Belzer Rav read 'al er'eh b'mos hayeled' with a cry. He concludes that a word of a tzaddik can break the heart, and one must guard oneself from hearing words against emunah.

title.en: L'chaim and singing

summary.en: The Mashgiach tells the bachurim to make brachos and say l'chaim to their friends, followed by singing.

oneLiner.en: Opening Tanya chapter 16, the Mashgiach explains that a Jew's service is to rule over nature, shown by Avraham's inherited emunah above understanding and by the mitzvah of milah, and made possible by the neshamah that stands above nature.

abstract.en: The Mashgiach reviews the end of Tanya chapter 15: true service of Hashem is the effort to go beyond routine, aroused either by contemplating Hashem's greatness or by stirring the hidden love inherited from Avraham Avinu. Opening chapter 16, which calls for ruling over the nature in the left chamber of the heart, he ties this to milah. A Jew's emunah is hereditary, like an animal's instinct, while a non-Jew is held responsible because an honest look at the world and at Sinai shows the truth. Avraham was a new species, given a new power of birth through the added hei. His mitzvos were emunah and milah: emunah begins where understanding ends, so milah comes at eight days, while Yishmael's empty milah waits for thirteen. After a long digression on Yishmael, Eretz Yisrael and the end of the exile, he returns: milah defies nature, and the neshamah, above nature, lets the mind rule the heart.

en: True service of Hashem is the effort that breaks routine and comfort, aroused either by contemplating Hashem's greatness or by stirring the hidden love in the heart.
A Jew's emunah is an inheritance from Avraham Avinu, hereditary like an animal's instinct, while a non-Jew is held responsible because honest observation of the world and of Sinai leads to the truth.
Emunah begins where understanding ends, and milah at eight days is the sign of this emunah above understanding.
Milah is the clearest illustration of a Jew's task to defy nature: right at birth one removes what nature produced.
A person can rule over nature because his neshamah, a part of G-d above, is above nature and shines into his nefesh, so the mind rules over the heart.

summary.en: The Mashgiach reviews that real service of Hashem is the extra effort beyond routine, and the two ways the Tanya gives to arouse it: contemplating Hashem's greatness, or stirring the hidden love inherited from Avraham Avinu.

title.en: Chapter 16: ruling nature; inherited emunah

summary.en: The Mashgiach opens chapter 16, that the main thing is to rule over nature, and links it to milah and to the emunah inherited from Avraham. He compares hereditary emunah to animal instinct and explains why a non-Jew is still responsible to believe.

title.en: Avraham, a new species of believer

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that a non-Jew's denial is rationalization to escape obligation, while Jews believe by inheritance. Avraham and Sarah were barren because Avraham was a new species, given a new power of birth with the added hei, and with him creation was completed.

title.en: Emunah and milah: above understanding

summary.en: After a question about Yishmael, the Mashgiach explains that Avraham's mitzvos are emunah and milah. Emunah starts where understanding ends, which is why milah is done at eight days without daas, while Yishmael's milah at thirteen is an empty milah that needs daas.

title.en: The eighth day and Yishmael's empty milah

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that milah is on the eighth day because the senses and intellect reach only the nature of the seven days of creation, while Jewish emunah is above nature. Yishmael's milah lacks the spiritual power of a Jew's, and the Zohar says he received Eretz Yisrael through it while it lies empty.

title.en: Digression: Yishmael and the end of exile

summary.en: In a long digression the Mashgiach speaks of Eretz Yisrael flourishing as a sign of Moshiach, of Yishmael as the adversary of Yitzchak and the last stage of the exile, and of Torah codes he heard from Rav Michoel Ber Weissmandl, pointing to a hint of Moshiach in this week's parsha.

title.en: Milah: the model of breaking nature

summary.en: Returning to the Tanya, the Mashgiach explains that nature dictates every creature's behavior and a Jew must rule above it. Milah removes the orlah that nature produces, and that power accompanies a Jew all his life: to get up when nature says sleep, and to check and sanctify himself even in what is permitted.

title.en: How a creature of nature rules nature

summary.en: The Mashgiach asks how a person, himself a product of nature, can defy it, and answers from the Tanya that the neshamah, a part of G-d above, shines into the nefesh, so the mind rules the heart. Contemplating Hashem's greatness in chochmah and binah gives birth to the middos and to withdrawing from evil.

oneLiner.en: The Mashgiach explains the war against Midian as a war of holiness against impurity fought with Torah and tefillah, says that today's war against the Jewish people is the same kind of war, and ties the haftarah of Yirmiyahu to the avodah of the Three Weeks.

abstract.en: The Mashgiach begins with the war against Midian in parshas Matos: only tzaddikim were drafted, it had to be led by Moshe Rabbeinu, and for every thousand who fought a thousand stayed back to daven, with the Aron, the Tzitz and the trumpets. Bringing a question of the Satmar Rav, why the Jews stayed pure in Egypt yet fell with Midian, he explains that Bilaam fought with the full power of kishuf and impurity, so the answer had to be a war of holiness. He then says the Torah is eternal: today the Sitra Achra wages that same war, not with the sword but with the tools of impurity, and the answer is Torah and tefillah. Turning to the haftarah, he brings the Chasam Sofer that Yirmiyahu was a gilgul of Shlomo HaMelech, who was a gilgul of Betzalel, and closes with the avodah of the Three Weeks: to turn these days into joy.

en: The war against Midian needed unusual preparations: tzaddikim instead of ordinary soldiers, Moshe Rabbeinu's leadership, a thousand davening for every thousand fighting, and the Aron, Tzitz and trumpets.
Midian did not fight with weapons but with impurity and Bilaam's kishuf, so it was a heavenly war of holiness against impurity.
The Torah is eternal, and today the Jewish people are living through the war of Midian again: a war of impurity rather than of the sword.
Against the tools of kishuf, the Jewish people must come with the holy vessels: the Urim is Torah, and the Tzitz and the trumpets are tefillah.
The avodah of the Three Weeks is to turn these days into joy, so that Yirmiyahu may again become Shlomo HaMelech singing Shir HaShirim in the Beis HaMikdash.

title.en: The war of Midian, a war of holiness

summary.en: Following the Nesivos Shalom, the Mashgiach describes the unusual preparations for the war against Midian and brings the Satmar Rav's question why the Jews fell there after staying pure in Egypt. He answers that Bilaam fought with all the forces of kishuf and impurity, so the war had to be fought with holiness, as a last battle before entering Eretz Yisrael.

title.en: Today's war of Midian

summary.en: The Mashgiach says the Torah is eternal and that the Jewish people are living through the war of Midian today: not the sword of the long galus but the tools of impurity. The answer is the holy vessels, Torah and tefillah, and parshas Matos read this Shabbos gives strength for this war, which each person fights at his own level.

title.en: Yirmiyahu, Shlomo and the Three Weeks

summary.en: On the haftarah, the Mashgiach brings the Chasam Sofer that Yirmiyahu was a gilgul of Shlomo HaMelech, and Shlomo of Betzalel, explaining why Betzalel needed the people's consent and why Shlomo had to witness the churban. He closes with the avodah of the Three Weeks: to turn these days into joy, so that Yirmiyahu may again be Shlomo singing Shir HaShirim.

oneLiner.en: The Mashgiach explains that at his milah Avraham Avinu was remade by Hashem into a new creation who believes in the Ribono shel Olam by nature, and that this emunah passes to his children by inheritance, the way animals inherit instinctive knowledge.

abstract.en: The Mashgiach announces that this year he will speak about emunah, the foundation of all the mitzvos. The Rambam counts 'Anochi Hashem Elokecha' as the mitzvah of emunah, connected to Avraham, the first believer, whose emunah was simple, without chochmah. The Ramban holds that emunah is not one of the 613 but their foundation, like the foundation of a house, and the Mashgiach argues the Ramban seems right, since every mitzvah is phrased as a command while 'Anochi' is a statement. To defend the Rambam he builds a long introduction: bodily features and middos are inherited, learned knowledge is not, yet animals such as the bee, the beaver and the spider are born with knowledge. Avraham was a new creation: at his milah Hashem gave him the letter heh and made him a being who believes instinctively, and he was first made barren to cut him off from Terach. Every Jew inherits this emunah, which raises a question about Jews who deny it, left for next week.

en: The Rambam counts 'Anochi Hashem' as the mitzvah of emunah, while the Ramban holds emunah is not one of the 613 but the foundation on which all of them stand.
Every mitzvah in the Torah is written as a command, while 'Anochi Hashem' is a statement in which Hashem presents Himself, so the Mashgiach says the Ramban appears to be right.
Bodily features and character traits pass from parents to children, but learned knowledge does not; animals, however, are born with knowledge of how to build a hive, a dam or a web.
At his milah Hashem remade Avraham Avinu into a new creation who believes in the Ribono shel Olam by nature, not only through his intellect.
This emunah passes by inheritance to all of Avraham's children, who are therefore believers the sons of believers.

title.en: The mitzvah of emunah and Avraham

summary.en: The Mashgiach says that this year he will speak about emunah, the foundation of all the mitzvos. He brings 'Anochi Hashem' as the mitzvah of emunah according to the Rambam and ties it to Avraham Avinu, whose emunah was simple, without chochmah, like that of our grandmothers.

title.en: Rambam and Ramban: is emunah a mitzvah?

summary.en: The Mashgiach presents the Ramban's view that emunah is not one of the 613 mitzvos but their foundation, like the foundation of a house. He argues that the Ramban seems right: every mitzvah is phrased as a command, while 'Anochi Hashem' is a statement, like a doctor introducing himself.

title.en: What a child inherits from his parents

summary.en: To answer for the Rambam the Mashgiach begins a long introduction: features of the body, such as skin color, and traits of the soul, such as a quick temper, are inherited. Knowledge, such as knowing Bava Metzia by heart, is not inherited; it is acquired through toil in learning.

title.en: Inborn knowledge: bee, beaver and spider

summary.en: The Mashgiach shows that there is knowledge that is inherited: the bee builds its precise honeycomb, the beaver builds a dam, and the spider spins its species' web, though none was ever taught. He concludes that such knowledge is part of the creature's very being and passes on by inheritance.

title.en: Avraham Avinu as a new creation

summary.en: The Mashgiach says two things were created after the creation of the world: fire on motzaei Shabbos, and Avraham Avinu, a new creation whose novelty is his knowledge of Hashem. Others are punished for not believing because they could know through contemplating the world but do not want to; Avraham was remade at his milah to believe by nature, and the Mashgiach begins to explain the small heh of 'behibaram' as the letter of birth.

title.en: The heh of birth and Avraham's new name

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that the world was completed when Avraham received the heh at his bris. He shows the heh as the letter of birth from Rachel, whose name lacks a heh, from a segulah of a silver heh, and from 'hei lachem zera', and brings the verses in davening about Avraham's new name and his faithful heart: the new thing in him, emunah, passes to his children.

title.en: Cut off from Terach; a question for next week

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that Avraham was created barren to sever him from the generations of Terach, so that a new people believing in Hashem would begin from him, and he brings Rashi on why Terach's death is written before Avraham leaves. He ends with a strong question: if every Jew inherits emunah, how can there be Jews who deny Hashem? The answer is left for next week.

catalogTitle: אהבה ויראה שכליות מביאה את האדם לתשובה. רשע ורע לו אין לו אפשרות להיות עובד ה' אלא ע"י תשובה תתאה.

oneLiner.en: The Mashgiach explains how a beinoni whose heart cannot be stirred to feel love of Hashem can still serve Him through love and fear that he understands with his mind, and how Hashem joins that intellectual love to his mitzvos so they rise above.

abstract.en: The Mashgiach reads the opening of Tanya chapter 16: the great rule for a beinoni is that the mind rules the heart, so that contemplating Hashem's greatness arouses love and fear. Most people, however, understand but cannot feel; the Tanya's note traces this to a soul still in the stage of 'ibur', not yet 'born'. Such a person still understands that his soul should long to leave the body and cleave to Hashem, like a 'living widow' kept from her husband, and that the only contact is Torah and mitzvos. The Mashgiach brings stories of souls nearly leaving the body in dveikus, and the principle of 'ratzo vashov'. Acting on this intellectual love gives the mitzvos the two wings of love and fear. Since thought is too high to clothe a physical deed, Hashem 'combines' it with the deed beyond nature, as Chazal say of a good thought, lifting such mitzvos to the world of Beriah.

en: The Mashgiach explains the rule for the beinoni: action should flow from the mind, which contemplates Hashem's greatness and sends its message down to arouse love and fear in the heart.
Most people cannot turn understanding into felt love, because their soul is from the stage of 'ibur', still hidden like a fetus and not yet revealed.
Such a person still understands that his soul, sent down from the Kisei HaKavod, is like a 'living widow' longing for her husband, and that its only contact with Hashem is through Torah and mitzvos.
When he does mitzvos because of this intellectual love and fear, they act as the two wings that lift the mitzvos above, as if he felt real love.
By nature, love that is only in the mind cannot be the shliach of a physical deed, since only the heart is both physical and spiritual; Hashem combines it with the deed beyond nature.
Mitzvos done by habit, with no love or fear even in the mind, stop in a lower world, while those done with intellectual love and fear reach the world of Beriah.

title.en: The mind should rule the heart

summary.en: The Mashgiach reads the opening of the chapter, the great rule for the beinoni that the mind directs the heart. He contrasts a 'seichel nivdal', an intellect untouched by emotion, with the common case where laziness bends the mind to justify putting off davening.

title.en: Those who understand but cannot feel

summary.en: The Mashgiach describes the desired path, where the mind's contemplation stimulates love of Hashem in the heart, and says most people cannot reach it. He explains that souls pass through stages like conception, pregnancy and birth, and a soul sent down before its 'birth' cannot produce felt love, so it serves Hashem from understanding alone.

title.en: Love hidden in the mind: the soul of ibur

summary.en: Reading the Tanya, the Mashgiach explains that such a person's love stays hidden and never flames in the heart. The Tanya's note gives the reason: his soul is from the stage of 'ibur', not yet revealed. Still he understands that his soul should long to leave the body and cleave to Hashem.

title.en: Ratzo vashov: souls that nearly flew out

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that Hashem made the world run on 'ratzo vashov', running and returning, so no one may let his soul rush out in love. He tells of a tzaddik who played with his pocket watch in Shemoneh Esrei to keep his soul in his body, and brings a sefer that Avraham's words 'we will return' kept his soul in him at the Akeidah, while Sarah's soul left her when she heard of it.

title.en: The soul as a 'living widow'

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that the soul, which comes from the Kisei HaKavod, is held in the body against its will like a 'living widow' whose husband is alive but barriers keep her from him. He adds that in galus the tzaddikim long for Hashem more than in the time of the Beis HaMikdash, like a thirsty man in the desert without water.

title.en: Torah and mitzvos: the only contact

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that the soul in the body can grasp Hashem only through Torah and mitzvos, citing the earlier chapters' parable of one who embraces the king through his garments. One who understands this with his mind, and makes his mouth and limbs act on it, gives his mitzvos wings even without felt love.

title.en: The two wings and the Ba'al Shem Tov's shul

summary.en: The Mashgiach brings the Zohar that love and fear are the two wings that lift mitzvos, and tells of the Ba'al Shem Tov who could not enter a shul packed with mitzvos done without love and fear. He explains that intellectual love counts as these wings, which is why Chassidus dwells so much on the greatness of Hashem, and that without it a person would follow his body's pleasures.

title.en: Why 'combines' it with the deed

summary.en: The Mashgiach brings Chazal that Hashem combines a good thought with the deed, and asks why they did not simply say He credits it as if it were done. He explains that felt love and fear give the mitzvah life because the heart is a physical organ that also holds spiritual emotion, so it can be the shliach of the limbs, as the Gemara shows from the kohanim as shluchim of Hashem.

title.en: Why the mind cannot be the shliach

summary.en: Reading the Tanya, the Mashgiach explains that the heart, physical like the other limbs yet inward, can carry love and fear into the deed. Love that stays in the mind is far higher than the deed and cannot clothe it, so by nature it could not lift the mitzvah; it does so only because Hashem combines it.

title.en: Hashem joins thought to deed

summary.en: The Mashgiach answers the question: Hashem, Who can do anything, goes beyond nature and joins the intellectual love to the deed, as the Rema explains that He joins the spiritual soul to the physical body. Mitzvos done this way reach the world of Beriah, while mitzvos done by rote, with the mind on business, go up only to a lower world.

oneLiner.en: The Mashgiach teaches bachurim, from a letter of the Ba'al HaTanya, why a tzibbur should daven aloud, together and word by word around a fitting chazan.

abstract.en: Continuing last week's talk on tefillah, the Mashgiach recalls the Ramban that the world was created so that Jews should daven and proclaim aloud that they are Hashem's creations, and the Ba'al HaTanya's call to daven aloud around the chazan. He then reads a letter in which the Ba'al HaTanya begs his chassidim to daven together, word by word, as Klal Yisroel sang the Shirah at the sea. To explain why, he shows that every word of davening carries great depth: lashon hakodesh is Hashem's language, tzaddikim speak a holy language others cannot follow, as a story of the Sanzer Rav and the Ruzhiner shows, and the Chasam Sofer brings from the Ba'al Shem Tov that every word is a heichal. He discusses who should go to the amud, the Ba'al HaTanya's takanos for chazanim, why the crowd and chazan strengthen each other like the angels, answers objections to loud davening, and closes with a story of R' Aharon of Karlin and a call to daven aloud with nusach without disturbing others.

en: The Mashgiach brings the Ramban that the world was created so that Jews should daven and proclaim aloud that they are Hashem's creations.
The Ba'al HaTanya asks that the whole tzibbur daven together, saying each word at the same time, not one here and one there.
Every word of davening is a heichal above, so when all say the same word together the whole tzibbur stands in one heichal.
The amud is not ownerless; the chazan must be someone who can daven with geshmak and nusach and lift up the tzibbur.
When the crowd davens aloud it strengthens the chazan and his loud davening strengthens them, as the angels receive from one another.
One should daven aloud with the tzibbur and its nusach, but not shout off-tune in a way that disturbs others.

title.en: Davening aloud and together

summary.en: The Mashgiach recalls last week's Ramban and Tanya on davening aloud around the chazan, then reads a letter of the Ba'al HaTanya begging his chassidim to daven together word by word, as Klal Yisroel sang the Shirah at the sea.

title.en: The holy language of tzaddikim

summary.en: He explains that every word of davening has great depth: lashon hakodesh is Hashem's language, as Yosef told his brothers, and tzaddikim speak in a holy language others cannot follow, shown by a story of the Sanzer Rav's visit to the Ruzhiner.

title.en: Every word is a heichal

summary.en: The Mashgiach brings the Chasam Sofer quoting the Ba'al Shem Tov that every word of davening is a heichal, and explains that this is why the Ba'al HaTanya wants all to say each word together; he criticizes latecomers and talking or silence during davening.

title.en: Who should go to the amud

summary.en: Following the Ba'al HaTanya, the Mashgiach says the amud is not ownerless: only one who can daven with nusach and geshmak and lift up the tzibbur should go, even on a yahrzeit, and he tells the bachurim to remember this when they are older.

title.en: The Ba'al HaTanya's takanos for chazanim

summary.en: The Mashgiach reads the Ba'al HaTanya's advice to appoint set, fitting chazanim who daven word by word aloud without rushing, a weekday davening of about an hour and a half, and his cry of 'gevald' over chazanim who rush.

title.en: Gathering around the chazan, like the angels

summary.en: He explains why the tzibbur gathers around the chazan: the loud crowd and the chazan strengthen each other, as the angels receive from one another and as the Shirah was sung together; he answers those who object to loud davening with a comparison to the shouting at a baseball game and calls for a good eye toward others.

title.en: R' Aharon of Karlin and davening with nusach

summary.en: The Mashgiach tells of R' Aharon of Karlin, whose loud davening brought him before a beis din, and concludes that one should daven aloud with the tzibbur and its nusach, while someone without a good voice should not shout and disturb others.

oneLiner.en: The Mashgiach speaks to bachurim about the danger of jealousy and of shaming another person, through Rebbe Elimelech's tefillah, the story of Kayin and a series of stories of tzaddikim.

abstract.en: The Mashgiach opens with the line in Rebbe Elimelech's tefillah asking to be saved from jealousy, which he calls the hardest thing in the world and common at every age. He traces kinah from creation: the moon envied the sun, the nachash envied Adam, and Kayin, a great man to whom Hashem spoke, killed Hevel out of envy. Through the Midrash on 'Am I my brother's keeper?' he shows Kayin blaming Hashem for the trait. Kinah led to the sale of Yosef and the churban. He tells bachurim to say that part of the tefillah many times. He then turns to bein adam lachaveiro: the Chernobyler who protected a thief from shame, the Berditchever on the matzah bakers' widows, and the Chasam Sofer's responsum about reburying Reb Mordechai Banet, who was penalized for shaming a kallah though he was right. Reb Shlomo Bloch's story of a young ilui who shamed a rav, and Reb Hershele Rimanover's story with the Yeshuos Yaakov, close the shiur.

en: Kinah is the hardest trait in the world; it is found at every age and even among tzaddikim, and it goes back to creation.
Kayin was a great man, yet jealousy brought him to kill his brother; jealousy also caused the sale of Yosef and, with sinas chinam, the churban.
Rebbe Elimelech's tefillah asks to see the virtues of one's friends and not their faults, and the Mashgiach tells a bachur struggling with jealousy to say it many times.
Good middos between man and his fellow include taking great care never to shame another person.
Even when a person is right, shaming someone carries a heavy price, as with Reb Mordechai Banet and the young ilui.
One who is careful with the honor of others merits all the blessings.

title.en: Kinah from creation to Kayin

summary.en: The Mashgiach opens with the plea against jealousy in Rebbe Elimelech's tefillah, calls kinah the hardest thing in the world, and traces it from the moon and the sun through the nachash to Kayin, a great man to whom Hashem spoke before and after he killed Hevel.

title.en: Kayin's complaint and Rebbe Elimelech's tefillah

summary.en: The Mashgiach contrasts the cheder translation of 'Am I my brother's keeper?' with the Midrash, where Kayin asks Hashem why He gave him such jealousy. He shows kinah behind the sale of Yosef and the churban, explains Rebbe Elimelech's plea to see others' virtues, tells bachurim to say it many times, and tells how Reb Aharon Roth praised the Vizhnitzer Rebbe for being free of jealousy.

title.en: The Chernobyler's spoon and the Berditchever's matzos

summary.en: Turning to good middos between man and his fellow, the Mashgiach tells how the Chernobyler said he gave a stolen silver spoon to a poor man rather than shame him, and how the Berditchever Rav warned the matzah bakers not to put the blood of the overworked widows into their matzos.

title.en: The Chasam Sofer and Reb Mordechai Banet's grave

summary.en: The Mashgiach tells the story behind a responsum of the Chasam Sofer about reburying Reb Mordechai Banet, the Rav of Nikolsburg. The ruling waited six months because Reb Mordechai Banet came to him in a dream: he had to lie six months beside a kallah he had shamed by breaking off a shidduch, though he had been right al pi halachah.

title.en: The ilui who shamed a rav

summary.en: The Mashgiach tells Reb Shlomo Bloch's story of a seventeen-year-old ilui who refuted a visiting rav's pilpul in public and shamed him; he grew into a gadol but never had children, which Reb Shlomo Bloch called his punishment. The Mashgiach concludes that care for the honor of others brings all blessings.

title.en: Reb Hershele Rimanover and the Yeshuos Yaakov

summary.en: The Mashgiach tells how Reb Hershele, a tailor's son, became the shamash and then the successor of Reb Mendel of Rimanov, and how the Yeshuos Yaakov, who would not honor him, removed the chairs, until Reb Hershele stopped at the doorway and the mezuzah was found to be pasul.

oneLiner.en: The Mashgiach explains why a rotzeach (killer) is sent to the cities of the Levi'im: every life is a song to Hashem, the killer cut off another's song, and the Levi'im, masters of song, reawaken his life, as Shabbos does for every Jew.

abstract.en: The Mashgiach opens with the Shem MiShmuel in the name of his father, the Avnei Nezer: a killer took life from another, so life is taken from him, and he must go to the cities of the Levi'im so that they can give him life again. To explain this, the Mashgiach teaches that all of creation sings to Hashem with the seven 'voices' of Tehillim 29, and that a person's life itself is his song. The killer cut off another Jew's song, so his own song falls silent, like the sun that Yehoshua stopped. The Levi'im's song is tuned to every Jewish soul, as a tuning fork sets off a piano and as the north wind played David's harp at midnight, and so it reawakens the killer. Every sin holds something of killing, and Shabbos, when Gan Eden comes down, is a city of refuge that makes every Jewish heart sing, above all on the Shabbosos of the Three Weeks.

en: Following the Avnei Nezer, a killer took life from another, so life is taken from him, and the Levi'im must give him life again.
All of creation sings to Hashem with seven voices, and each person's life is his own song.
The killer cut off another's song, so his own song is silenced, like the sun at Givon.
The song of the Levi'im is tuned to every Jewish soul and so it can reawaken the killer's life.
Shabbos, when Gan Eden comes down to the world, is a city of refuge for every sinner and makes every Jewish heart sing.

title.en: The killer and the song of life

summary.en: The Mashgiach brings the Avnei Nezer that a killer must go to the cities of the Levi'im to receive life from them, and begins to explain it: all of creation sings to Hashem with the seven voices, and a person's life is his song, which the killer cut off.

title.en: The silenced sun and the Levi'im's song

summary.en: The Mashgiach compares the killer to the sun that Yehoshua silenced, explains that the Levi'im are the masters of song, and uses a tuning fork and David's harp that played by itself at midnight to show how the Levi'im's song reawakens the killer's soul.

title.en: Shabbos as the city of refuge

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that on Shabbos Gan Eden comes down and every Jewish heart sings, that Kabbalas Shabbos completes the seven voices, and that Shabbos is a city of refuge for every sin; he ends with the special greatness of the Shabbosos of the Three Weeks.

catalogTitle: ביאור על תשובה תתאה. עצה למי שאפילו אהבה שכליות אינו יכול לפועל בעצמו. כי קרוב אליך בדרך קצרה - יותר קלה לחלושי כח ע"י האהבה המתוסרת בלבו.

oneLiner.en: The Mashgiach explains Tanya chapter 17: why 'the thing is very near to you' is true for every Jew through the mind's rule over the heart, why it does not speak to a true rasha, and how even he returns through the lower teshuvah that raises the fallen Hei.

abstract.en: The Mashgiach reviews the previous chapter: one who cannot turn intellectual love and fear into emotion may serve with the mind alone, since some souls are still 'in the womb'. Chapter 17 now applies these ideas to the verse the Tanya's title page names as its purpose, 'ki karov eilecha'. Our senses seem to deny it, since a complete turning of the heart is rare: love cannot be divided, and one who still craves worldly pleasure does not truly love Hashem. He tells stories of tzaddikim who no longer tasted food. The Gemara's 'yirah is a small thing' applies to Moshe Rabbeinu, and what is asked of everyone is action driven by the mind. Logical love, like a mother's love she does not feel, is within every person's power, because the mind rules the heart by nature, except in the true rasha, whose lost control is a punishment. Such a rasha needs teshuvah first: a broken heart, often aroused from above, the lower teshuvah that raises the fallen Hei, connected to Chanukah.

en: One whose soul cannot produce emotional love and fear may serve Hashem with the understanding of the mind alone; not everyone is required to reach the same level.
Love cannot be divided: one who still pursues worldly pleasure and believes he also loves Hashem fully is deceiving himself.
What 'ki karov' promises every Jew is not a transformed heart but mitzvos done because the mind understands the duty.
A person can think as much as he wants even when he cannot love as much as he wants, so logical love is within everyone's reach.
By nature the mind rules the heart and the limbs, except in a true rasha, who as a punishment for his sins has lost that control.
A true rasha cannot begin serving Hashem without first breaking the barrier of the kelipos through a broken heart; this is the lower teshuvah, which returns the lower Hei of Hashem's Name.

title.en: Review: serving with the mind alone

summary.en: The Mashgiach reviews the previous chapter: Chochmah and Binah meditating on Hashem's greatness should stir love and fear in the heart, but one who cannot may serve with the mind's understanding alone. Such a soul is still 'in the womb' of Knesses Yisroel and not yet 'born', so revealed love is not required of it.

title.en: Chapter 17 and the verse 'ki karov'

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that chapter 17 begins a new phase, applying the earlier axioms in practice, and that the title page names the verse 'ki karov eilecha' as the Tanya's purpose. He raises the difficulty that our senses seem to deny it, and rejects the idea that it applied only to Moshe Rabbeinu's generation: the Torah speaks to every generation and every person.

title.en: Love cannot be divided

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains why turning the heart from worldly desire to true love of Hashem is so hard: love is indivisible and can be directed to only one object. With the example of enjoying an ice cream, he says that one who still desires worldly pleasure and thinks he also loves Hashem is imagining it, though thinking of Hashem while eating is better than nothing.

title.en: Tzaddikim beyond the taste of food

summary.en: The Mashgiach says the Ba'al HaTanya and his chassidim experienced this level, and tells of tzaddikim in recent times: one who said he had not known the taste of food for twenty years, two Rebbes recalling the wartime transports, and the Yismach Moshe, who ate dishwater thinking it was soup. He ends that one who still enjoys the ice cream should not fool himself that his love of Hashem is complete.

title.en: 'Yirah is a small thing' for Moshe

summary.en: The Mashgiach brings the Gemara that calls yirah a small thing for Moshe Rabbeinu, and explains that a complete transformation of the heart belongs to tzaddikim like Dovid HaMelech, not to beinonim. What Hashem asks of everyone, as the previous chapters explained, is enough yirah in the mind to drive the doing.

title.en: Doing the mitzvah from the mind's duty

summary.en: The Mashgiach stresses that the Tanya does not say to refrain from the ice cream; it says that when a mitzvah comes, the mind should recognize the duty and act. His example is tefillin: one may not feel the glow, but feels the obligation because Hashem requires it, and this suffices for a soul from ibbur rather than leidah.

title.en: Logical love is in every person's power

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that the level near to everyone is a logical love, even if it is not revealed in the heart like flames of fire, because the mind is in a person's power: he cannot love as he wishes but can think as he wishes. He compares it to a mother's love that she does not always feel, and says the felt joy of the mitzvah is its reward, granted to tzaddikim but not required of everyone in this world.

title.en: The mind rules the heart, except in a rasha

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that by nature the mind controls the heart, the mouth and the limbs, except in a true rasha, who has lost that control; he brings Chazal that the wicked are in the power of their heart and the heart of tzaddikim is in their power, and the question of Pharaoh's hardened heart. He explains the loss of control as a punishment that began with free choice, comparing it to a case in the Gemara that starts with negligence and ends with compulsion, and concludes that 'ki karov' does not speak to such reshaim, who are called dead in their lifetime.

title.en: How a rasha begins: a broken heart

summary.en: The Mashgiach asks how one who lost his free choice can do teshuvah, and answers that every Jew has a point that evil cannot touch, which Hashem sometimes arouses through circumstances. A rasha can do a mitzvah here and there, but to begin real service he must first break the iron wall of the kelipos with a broken heart; this is the lower teshuvah, as opposed to the higher teshuvah from love.

title.en: Raising the fallen Hei; Chanukah

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that sin separates the lower Hei, the Shechinah, from the Name, dragging it into exile with the person, and teshuvah, 'tashuv Hei', returns it. He connects this to Chanukah of the coming month Kislev: the wicks and oils that do not burn on Shabbos burn on Chanukah, since then Hashem comes down to lift the fallen; he ends with the Tanya's description of the rasha's soul in exile.

oneLiner.en: The Mashgiach explains that a Jew's emunah is a feeling of the heart inherited from the mother, so that even a Jew who denies Hashem is only rationalizing what he knows deep inside.

abstract.en: The Mashgiach opens by contrasting a gentile, who can grasp emunah through logic, with a Jew, who feels it by instinct. He illustrates with the halacha of a burglar: a son may not kill his father who breaks in, because a father's heart feels for his son even when he does not know whose house it is. From there he distinguishes chochmah, fixed facts that all agree on, from binah, the understanding of the heart, which Chazal say was given more to women; the seder's three matzos and four cups reflect this. Jewishness follows the mother because emunah is a feeling, and he shows from Hebrew grammar that the root of emunah yields the word for mother. He then describes how people rationalize out of pride, from the fox and the grapes, Eisav and a bochur blaming his rebbe, and concludes that a Jewish apikores really believes but denies out of desire, illustrated by a letter written after the Six Day War.

en: A gentile can understand emunah with logic, but a Jew feels it instinctively in his heart.
Chochmah is fixed knowledge all must accept, while binah is the heart's understanding, which differs from person to person according to his nature.
A child's Jewishness follows the mother because emunah is a feeling, and feeling comes from the mother.
A person's pride drives him to justify himself and blame anything but himself, which psychology calls rationalization and denial.
A Jewish apikores truly believes; he denies only because he wants to follow his desires.

title.en: Emunah as instinct: the father and the burglar

summary.en: The Mashgiach opens by saying a Jew feels emunah instinctively, unlike a gentile who reaches it through logic. He brings the halacha of a burglar who may be killed, and Rashi's case of a father breaking in to his son, and argues that even a father who does not know it is his son's house feels it in his heart, as even wild animals do for their young.

title.en: Chochmah and binah, matzos and cups

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that Jews are Hashem's children and feel bound to Him with the heart, not only the mind. He contrasts chochmah, objective facts, with binah, the heart's understanding, reads 'aliba d'Abaye' as 'according to Abaye's heart', and brings the Gemara that women were given extra binah. The three matzos (grain, intellect) and four cups (wine, feeling) at the seder, matching the Avos and Imahos, show the two sides.

title.en: A wife's feeling and the Lechovitcher's cry

summary.en: The Mashgiach brings the Avnei Nezer's explanation of why a woman may remarry on one witness's word: she feels whether her husband is alive. He then tells how Reb Mordechai of Lechovitch cried out that he no longer felt his Rebbe, Reb Shlomo of Karlin, until he was told the Rebbe had passed away.

title.en: Why Jewishness follows the mother: emunah and em

summary.en: The Mashgiach asks why a child's Jewishness follows the mother when tribe and inheritance follow the father, and answers that emunah is a feeling, which comes from the mother. He supports this from a rule of Hebrew grammar: a three-letter verb ending in nun drops it as a noun (chanan to chen, shanan to shen, ganan to gan), so from aman, to believe, comes em, mother.

title.en: Ben Sira's fox and the sour grapes

summary.en: The Mashgiach mentions the Gemara on outside books, among them Ben Sira's fables, which the gentiles adopted as Aesop's fables. He tells the fable of the fox who could not climb the fence to the grapes and declared them sour, and explains that like every proud person the fox cannot admit his own weakness.

title.en: Eisav, the hammer and the bochur: rationalization

summary.en: The Mashgiach says that everything, even psychology, can be learned from Chumash and Rashi, and shows it with Eisav: seeing that his Canaanite wives displeased his parents, he concluded he lost the berachos because of his wives and married Yishmael's daughter. He adds the man who hits his thumb and blames the hammer and the bochur who blames his rebbe and classroom, calling this rationalization born of pride.

title.en: The Jewish apikores really believes

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that a Jewish apikores denies Hashem only because he wants to follow his desires, cites a philosopher's essay that there never was a true atheist, and tells of the miracles of the Six Day War and a woman who wrote to a newspaper asking it to stop reporting them so she could keep going to the beach on Shabbos. He concludes that every Jew believes.

oneLiner.en: The Mashgiach teaches the bachurim that coming early and acting with zerizus shows that the avodah is precious to a person, opens the gates of Heaven for him, and is the special task of the last generation before Moshiach.

abstract.en: The Mashgiach opens with a letter of Rabbi Yonasan Eybeschutz, who wrote that his true portion from all his toil was the time he stood before Hashem in tefillah, even as others laughed at how long he davened. He asks why a giant in learning would say this, and answers that davening is dveykus, closeness to Hashem, and urges davening together with the tzibbur. He then brings the Gemara at the end of Sukkah about the mishmar of Bilgah, whose window in the Beis Hamikdash was closed because they came late, and explains that lateness shows the avodah is not precious to a person, so Heaven closes its gates to him. Applying this to the Bnei Dan, who lagged behind the camp and were struck by Amalek, he says our generation, the last, must repair their flaw with zerizus, which hastens Moshiach. He ends with the souls that came to the Chiddushei HaRim on erev Shabbos, one of them too late.

en: Davening is dveykus, a person's direct closeness to Hashem, which is why Rabbi Yonasan Eybeschutz called his time in tefillah his true portion.
Coming late shows that the avodah is not precious to a person, as the Gemara shows with the mishmar of Bilgah.
Whoever is late loses his flow of blessing from Heaven, while one who comes early finds the gates of Torah and tefillah opened for him.
Our generation corresponds to the Bnei Dan at the rear of the camp, and its task is to repair their lack of zerizus.
Each Jew has a mitzvah that is the root of his soul, recognized by his desire for it and by the obstacles that block it.
Zerizus in davening and learning can bring Moshiach sooner.

the root mitzvah of each soul
tikkun of souls on erev Shabbos

title.en: Rabbi Yonasan Eybeschutz's portion in tefillah

summary.en: The Mashgiach brings a letter of Rabbi Yonasan Eybeschutz, printed in Yaaros Devash, telling a student that while he was still davening, the tzibbur was already done and young people laughed at him, yet this was his portion from all his toil. He asks how a giant in Torah could say his portion was tefillah rather than learning.

title.en: Davening is dveykus; davening together

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that the mitzvos are counsels for coming close to Hashem, that learning demands concentration on the sugya while davening is dveykus, as the Shulchan Aruch HaRav allows one who has learned much to devote time to dveykus. He describes davening in Stolin and among Sefardim, all together like the angels, and repeats that one should daven together with the tzibbur.

title.en: The mishmar of Bilgah came late

summary.en: The Mashgiach brings the Gemara at the end of Sukkah: each of the twenty-four mishmaros had its own window for its vessels, and Bilgah's was closed because they came late, so they had to borrow vessels. He explains that coming late shows the avodah is not precious to them, just as bachurim late for davening are on time for a trip.

title.en: A closed window, a closed heart

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains the punishment: whoever comes late shows the avodah is not dear to him, so Heaven closes his flow of blessing, while for one who comes early the gates of Torah and tefillah open. What is in Heaven is in man; a closed heart is a closed window, and a bachur who comes late should make a cheshbon hanefesh and warm himself with mussar and Chassidus.

title.en: The Bnei Dan and our generation

summary.en: The Mashgiach describes how the stragglers of Dan, slow to pack when the camp moved, fell outside the clouds of glory and were attacked by Amalek. Since the camp in space is also a camp in time, the generation of Moshe Rabbeinu is the front and the generation of Moshiach is Dan at the rear, so we must repair their lack of zerizus.

title.en: Each soul's mitzvah and zerizus for Moshiach

summary.en: The Mashgiach brings the rule that every Jew has a mitzvah that is his soul's root, recognized by his desire for it and by the difficulties the yetzer hara puts in its way, and that every generation has such a mitzvah too, as with tzitzis. Our generation's is emunah and zerizus: the Gemara on 'b'itah achishena' shows Moshiach can come sooner, and Amalek, who 'cooled' Israel on the way, is answered with warmth and zerizus.

title.en: The soul that came late on erev Shabbos

summary.en: The Mashgiach tells how souls came to the Chiddushei HaRim on erev Shabbos for a tikkun, and once he told a soul it was too late, since the Rebbetzin had already lit candles. He explains that a soul which was slow in life arrives late after life too, and closes that our generation's task is to be mezarez in Torah and tefillah and bring Moshiach.

oneLiner.en: Through a chain of true stories about gedolim, the Mashgiach shows bachurim how grave it is to shame another Jew and how far great people went to spare others even a moment of distress.

abstract.en: The Mashgiach opens by stressing that the stories he tells come from reliable sources. He tells of a brilliant Slabodka bachur who publicly exposed a friend's borrowed chiddush and, though he became a gadol, died childless; the mashgiach there saw it as punishment for shaming another. He then tells of a soul that came to Reb Moshe of Savran for a tikkun because its owner had shamed a chassan before his father-in-law. A series of stories about Reb Akiva Eiger follows: honoring the Rav of Lissa, hiding his greatness during another chassan's sheva brachos, spilling his own wine to cover a guest's mishap, and conceding a kashya to Reb Mordechai Benet in Nikolsburg. The shiur closes with Reb Yisrael Salanter: his call to account for rabbanim who did not teach middos, his view on asking forgiveness for lashon hara, and his shortening of a Shabbos meal for the sake of a tired maid.

en: The Mashgiach says that shaming another Jew in public is so grave that Chazal say such a person has no share in the World to Come, and the punishment can follow a person all his life.
He warns that young bachurim in particular must be very careful, because they do not yet grasp the severity of shaming another.
Even a correction that seems harmless, made in front of someone's father-in-law, can keep a soul out of Gan Eden.
Reb Akiva Eiger repeatedly gave up his own honor, even letting himself look unlearned, so that no one else would feel slighted.
The Mashgiach says it is better to suffer, even to throw oneself into a fiery furnace, than to shame another.
Reb Yisrael Salanter taught that sensitivity to others, such as a tired maid, comes before extra zemiros and divrei Torah at one's own table.

title.en: The Slabodka bachur who exposed a stolen chiddush

summary.en: The Mashgiach stresses that his stories come from reliable sources, then tells of a brilliant Slabodka bachur who bought copies of a sefer in Vilna to prove publicly that a rival's chiddush was copied. The mashgiach was deeply pained; the bachur became a gadol but died childless, and the Mashgiach warns bachurim to be very careful not to shame anyone.

title.en: A soul punished for shaming a chassan

summary.en: Reb Moshe of Savran told of a soul, a talmid chacham who had done teshuvah, kept out of Gan Eden because he had corrected a chassan's mistaken word in shul in front of his father-in-law. Along the way the Mashgiach tells how his own rebbe, Reb Shraga Feivel Mendlowitz, once corrected an old man's reading in shul and the man became angry.

title.en: Reb Akiva Eiger hides his greatness

summary.en: Reb Akiva Eiger asks the Rav of Lissa to forgive him for receiving the more honored aliyah in Posen. Then, as a young chassan, he gives only simple divrei Torah for a whole Shabbos, nearly losing his shidduch, so as not to outshine another newly engaged chassan in town until that chassan's sheva brachos ended.

title.en: The spilled wine and the kashya in Nikolsburg

summary.en: Reb Akiva Eiger spills his own cup at the Seder so a poor guest who stained the tablecloth would not be ashamed, and in Nikolsburg he lets a kashya of Reb Mordechai Benet stand in public, revealing the answer only privately so the local Rav would not be lowered. The Mashgiach concludes that great people had middos and derech eretz and would rather suffer than shame anyone.

title.en: Reb Yisrael Salanter on shaming and forgiveness

summary.en: Reb Yisrael Salanter leaves a yeshiva so a fellow maggid shiur would not be hurt, and after a wealthy man shames a former shoemaker at his daughter's wedding in Vilna, he says the rabbanim of the previous generation are being judged for not teaching good middos. The Mashgiach then describes Reb Yisrael Salanter's disagreement with the Chafetz Chaim on whether one must ask forgiveness for lashon hara when it would only cause the victim pain.

title.en: A two-hour seudah for the maid's sake

summary.en: A wealthy host describes his five-hour Shabbos meal with glatt kosher meat, zemiros and divrei Torah; the Mashgiach explains along the way what glatt kosher means and how it came to New York. Reb Yisrael Salanter agrees to come only if the meal lasts two hours, then asks the exhausted maid for forgiveness and shows the host that his extra zemiros came at her expense.

catalogTitle: ביאור חכמה ובינה. חכמה - שורש מחשבתו - י"ח כח מה. צריך להיות פתי בענין אמונה.

oneLiner.en: Opening Tanya chapter 18, the Mashgiach explains the 'short way' for small minds: the hidden love and emunah every Jew inherits from the Avos, rooted in the chochmah at the core of the soul that is bound to the Or Ein Sof.

abstract.en: The Mashgiach first completes the previous chapter: a ba'al teshuvah, having sunk into the depths of tumah, raises sparks of kedushah no tzaddik can reach, and he illustrates it with the story of the Bach in Gehinnom. Turning to chapter 18, he reviews the 'long way' of contemplation through chochmah and binah and introduces the 'short way' for small souls who cannot dwell on Hashem's greatness. Every Jew has a hidden love and natural emunah, an inheritance from the Avos, who are true fathers. A Jew who denies Hashem is like a sick stomach that has lost its appetite. The Avos were a merkavah for Hashem and passed this to all their descendants, down to the lowest soul, whose inner core is chochmah, bound to the Or Ein Sof, because souls are not created yesh me'ayin. From the Sefer HaGilgulim he explains how a rasha can beget a tzaddik, and how Moshiach's lineage was hidden in klippah from the Satan.

en: Tanya chapter 18 begins a 'short way' for people whose minds cannot dwell long on Hashem's greatness, after the 'long way' of chochmah and binah in the earlier chapters.
Every Jew has a hidden love and a natural emunah in Hashem, an inheritance from the Avos rather than something acquired.
Because the Avos were a merkavah for Hashem, they passed His powers on to all their descendants, even to the lowest soul of nefesh de'nefesh of Malchus de'Asiyah.
Hidden in every soul is chochmah, its inner core, in which the Or Ein Sof is clothed.
Jewish souls, unlike the rest of creation, are not made yesh me'ayin but are a direct extension from Hashem, like children.
Since even a rasha's inner core is bound to the Ein Sof, a rasha can sometimes beget a tzaddik far greater than himself.
